# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 1.220 urban, monastic, military and administrative settlement trajectories (5.829 settlement-year observations, mean 4,78 per centre) active across the 1.562.476 km² territory of Outer Mongolia between the foundation of the Mongol Empire in 1206AD and the establishment of the Bogd Khanate in 1912AD under JADE. Synthesising the Arts Council of Mongolia Documentation of Mongolian Monasteries (DOMM, 911 pre-1912 *khüree* and *khiid* monastic centres) [@DOMM2024Monasteries], the Tibetan Buddhist Resource Center (TBRC) monastery register [@Ryavec2014TBRC], OpenStreetMap and Wikidata historical site registers, mediaeval imperial archaeological excavations, Qing banner cadastres, Lifanyuan courier post registers and early twentieth-century geographical surveys [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @caoshuji2001zhongguo; @pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya; @Bemmann2020Karakorum], the register spans all six historical territories: Tüsheet Khan aimag (421 sites), Setsen Khan aimag (255), Sain Noyon Khan aimag (193), Khövsgöl and Dariganga (150), Zasagt Khan aimag (107) and Khovd frontier district (94). Across seven centuries of nomadic and sedentary settlement, the largest centres in the catalogue are Ulaanbaatar (Urga or Ikh Khüree, reaching 50k in 1911AD), the mediaeval imperial capital Karakorum (38k in 1255AD), Chinggis Khan's base camp Avraga Ord (14k in 1210AD), the Qing military seat Uliastai (8k in 1820AD), the Russian border trading depot Altanbulag (8k in 1860AD), the western frontier residency Khovd (6,8k in 1820AD), Tsetserleg (5,5k in 1850AD), Choibalsan (5k in 1911AD), Chinggis (4,2k in 1911AD) and Amarbayasgalant monastery (2,8k in 1820AD) [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya]. Beside the 1.220 included centres, the regional source ledger accounts for 338 excluded candidates (duplicate aliases and extralimital records) out of 1.558 total evaluated candidates (0 unaccounted).

# Background

Settlement patterns in Mongolia from 1206AD to 1912AD reflected two distinct urbanisation waves separated by centuries of nomadic pastoral circulation [@Bemmann2020Karakorum; @bawden1989modern]. In the thirteenth century, the unified Chinggisid state established fixed imperial capitals to house craft workshops, storehouses and diplomatic embassies, notably Avraga Ord along the Kherlen River and Karakorum in the Orkhon valley [@Wright2025Zuun; @Tolnai2026Tracing]. Following the collapse of the Yuan dynasty in 1368AD, these mediaeval urban hubs declined, and settlement resumed an almost exclusively mobile pastoral regime organised around mobile royal encampments (*ord*) [@bawden1989modern].

From the late sixteenth century onward, the widespread adoption of Tibetan Buddhism introduced a durable urban form: the permanent monastic enclave (*khüree* or *khiid*) [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @Ujeed2015Establishment]. Monasteries such as Erdene Zuu (founded 1586AD), Ikh Khüree (1639AD) and Amarbayasgalant (1727AD) evolved from mobile assemblies into stone and timber temple complexes flanked by permanent residential colleges, Chinese merchant quarters (*Maimaicheng*) and seasonal pastoral markets, anchoring the modern urban hierarchy of Outer Mongolia [@bawden1989modern; @maiskii1921sovremennaya].

# Methodology

Settlement records were compiled from the Arts Council of Mongolia Documentation of Mongolian Monasteries (DOMM, contributing 911 pre-1912 *khüree* and *khiid* monastic centres) [@DOMM2024Monasteries], the Tibetan Buddhist Resource Center (TBRC) monastery register [@Ryavec2014TBRC], OpenStreetMap and Wikidata Mongolian historical site inventories, China Historical GIS (CHGIS V6) administrative layers, archaeological excavation registers from the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, Qing Lifanyuan banner tables, and Russian field surveys by Aleksei Pozdneyev and Ivan Maiskii [@wusongdi2000zhongguo; @caoshuji2001zhongguo; @pozdneyev1971mongolia; @maiskii1921sovremennaya; @Bemmann2020Karakorum]. All 1.220 catalogued centres carry valid WGS84 geographic coordinates and 5.829 longitudinal population observations (mean 4,78 per centre) across historical benchmark years.

In the regional source ledger, 338 candidate records out of 1.558 total evaluated entries were categorised as excluded either as duplicate aliases situated close to higher-ranking canonical settlements (for instance, Kharkhorin and Erdene Zuu merged into Karakorum, Zayain Gegeniin Süm into Tsetserleg, Khuduu Aral into Tavan Khailaast, and Chinggis City into Chinggis) or as extralimital records lying outside the Outer Mongolian areal mask, ensuring zero double-counting and strict territorial bounds across the database.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exactly 1.220 included settlements (5.829 settlement-year observations, mean 4,78 per centre) and 338 excluded candidates out of 1.558 total evaluated candidates (0 unaccounted). All 1.220 catalogued centres map directly onto the six sub-regional territorial masks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-mongol} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading fifteen settlement population peaks.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-mongol} reports the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ranked by peak catalogued population, spanning mediaeval imperial capitals, Qing military headquarters, frontier trading marts and major Buddhist monastic centres.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("\\.", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e$population[[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(unlist(e$population)), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e$population))
  pk_y <- names(e$population)[which.max(unlist(e$population))]
  pk_v <- max(unlist(e$population))
  reg_nm <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[e$region_id]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e$name,
    Territory = reg_nm,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e$coords[[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e$coords[[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), "AD"),
    P1290 = get_pop_str(e, "1290"),
    P1820 = get_pop_str(e, "1820"),
    P1911 = get_pop_str(e, "1911"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in Mongolia from 1206AD to 1912AD ordered by peak catalogued population (n=1.220 total centres).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "1290AD", "1820AD", "1911AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-mongol} summarises settlement counts and leading centres across the six administrative territories. Tüsheet Khan aimag contained the highest concentration of catalogued sites (421), followed by Setsen Khan aimag (255), Sain Noyon Khan aimag (193) and Khövsgöl and Dariganga (150), with Zasagt Khan aimag (107) and the Khovd frontier district (94) spanning the west. Table \ref{tab:excluded-mongol} documents all 338 excluded candidates from the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e$region_id, rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(unlist(e$population)), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]]$name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = reg_short,
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement count and leading urban or monastic centre across all six territories from 1206AD to 1912AD (1.220 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Settlements", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c$status, "excluded"), ledger_data$candidates)
exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list, function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c$justification)
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  just <- gsub("-Mongolia", "", just, fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c$name,
    Territory = c$country,
    Category = "Duplicate alias",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "All 338 excluded candidates in the Mongolian source ledger, comprising duplicate aliases consolidated into canonical parent centres and extralimital records.",
  c("Candidate", "Country", "Reason", "Consolidation Note"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-mongol", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Three specific spatial constraints affect settlement analysis across historical Mongolia. First, monastic settlements frequently functioned as mobile tent camps before establishing permanent brick, stone or timber foundations [@pozdneyev1971mongolia; @bawden1989modern]. Ikh Khüree (Urga), for instance, moved across twenty-eight distinct geographic locations between 1639AD and 1778AD before permanently settling on the Tuul River, meaning its coordinates prior to 1778AD represent the institutional predecessor rather than a static geographic point.

Second, the 911 pre-1912 *khüree* and *khiid* complexes integrated from the DOMM survey [@DOMM2024Monasteries] and TBRC [@Ryavec2014TBRC] include numerous smaller seasonal or modest monastic assemblies whose early founding dates and resident clerical headcounts prior to late-nineteenth-century Russian surveys carry wider interpolation uncertainty. Third, purely nomadic pastoral seasonal camps leave minimal architectural surface remains outside hearth stones and corral lines [@DR2019Modeling; @Franklin2023Archaeology]. As a consequence, catalogued settlements capture nucleated monastic centres, imperial palaces, border fortresses and courier relay stations, while purely mobile pastoral populations are distributed via continuous kriging surfaces rather than nucleated town registers [@S2026Spatial].

# Conclusion

The settlement gazetteer of historical Mongolia illustrates the structural transformation of steppe urbanism from mediaeval imperial ords to eighteenth-century Buddhist monastic enclaves. Across 1.220 catalogued centres (5.829 settlement-year observations, mean 4,78 per centre), urban and monastic settlement concentrated along fertile river valleys (the Orkhon, Tuul, Kherlen and Selenge) and strategic trade arteries.

By 1912AD, the monastic metropolis of Ikh Khüree (50k) along with secondary hubs such as Uliastai (8k), Altanbulag (8k), Khovd (6,8k) and Tsetserleg (5,5k) formed a structured administrative network that underpinned the theocratic governance of the Bogd Khanate.
